cases.description: Shipped web defaults with inflation-escalated contributions.
cases.derivation: rho = 1.07/1.03 - 1 = 0.03883495145631066. n = ln((C + T*rho)/(C + PV*rho))/ln(1+rho) = ln(70601.9417/27883.4951)/ln(1.03883495) = 24.3838964605, so fireAge = 54.4. The projection crosses the 1.2M target between age 54 (1,173,603) and age 55 (1,243,180) in today's dollars, which is the crossing invariant from issue #46.

cases.description: Shipped web defaults with flat nominal contributions, whose purchasing power erodes.
cases.derivation: No closed form exists in today's dollars for a flat nominal contribution, so the deflated path (PV(1+r)^n + C((1+r)^n - 1)/r)/(1+i)^n is solved by bisection. Flat contributions must always reach FIRE no earlier than inflation-escalated ones.

cases.description: A scenario sharing no defaults with any other case, inflation-escalated.
cases.derivation: rho = 1.06/1.025 - 1. Same closed form as the defaults case; chosen so a drift in either implementation cannot hide behind a value that happens to be a shared default.

cases.description: The same non-default scenario with flat nominal contributions.
cases.derivation: Bisection on the deflated flat path, as in fire-defaults-flat.

cases.description: Return exactly equals inflation, so the real return is zero and the annuity factor is 0/0.
cases.derivation: r = i = 0.05 gives rho = 0 exactly. The closed form ((1+rho)^n - 1)/rho is undefined and its limit as rho -> 0 is the linear solution: 50,000 + 20,000n = 1,250,000 gives n = 60 exactly, so fireAge = 90. This is a live divide-by-zero that is currently special-cased correctly and must stay that way. Note the projection series is capped at 50 years, so it stops 10 years short of the crossing and the crossing invariant is not checkable here.

cases.description: A 2% return against 5% inflation. The target is genuinely unreachable, so Infinity is correct.
cases.derivation: rho = 1.02/1.05 - 1 = -0.02857142857142858 < 0, so B_{k+1} = B_k(1+rho) + C has a stable fixed point at B* = -C/rho = 20000/0.02857142857142858 = 700,000 exactly. The target is 50,000/0.04 = 1,250,000 > 700,000, so no finite n reaches it. Infinity is the mathematically correct answer and must not be 'fixed'.

cases.description: Current savings already exceed the FIRE number.
cases.derivation: PV >= target short-circuits to n = 0, so fireAge equals currentAge and no solving happens.

cases.description: $10,000 at 20% APR with a $500/month budget.
cases.derivation: Month-one interest is exactly 10000 * 0.20/12 = 166.666..., charged once and only once. Cross-checked against the amortization closed form n = -ln(1 - P*m/A)/ln(1+m) = 24.53, so 25 months. Pre-fix (#45) this wrongly reported 34 months, $6,617 of interest and $333.33 of month-one interest because interest was charged twice per month.

cases.description: Three debts cleared smallest-balance-first.
cases.derivation: Snowball orders by balance ascending, so the $1,500 debt clears first even though it carries the lowest rate. Total interest must be >= the avalanche case below.

cases.description: The same three debts cleared highest-rate-first.
cases.derivation: Avalanche orders by rate descending. Directing every spare dollar at the most expensive balance can never cost more total interest than any other ordering, so this must come in at or below debt-multi-snowball. A pre-fix bug inverted exactly this relationship.

cases.description: $1M at 4% with a 7% return and 3% inflation, over a 30 year horizon.
cases.derivation: The 3.88% real return roughly matches the 4% real draw, so the portfolio outlives the horizon and longevity is capped at retirementYears. The comparison table applies its own 50 year cap, so here the two legitimately report different caps rather than disagreeing.

cases.description: $1M at 5% with a 3% return and 3% inflation, over a 40 year horizon.
cases.derivation: Withdrawals grow at inflation while the portfolio grows at the same 3%, so the balance declines and is exhausted well before either cap binds. With neither cap active the headline longevity and the 5% row of the comparison table must agree exactly.

cases.description: Shipped Savings & Investment defaults: $100k plus $500/month for 30 years.
cases.derivation: Deflated closed form PV(1+rho)^30 + C((1+rho)^30 - 1)/rho with C = 6,000 and rho = 0.03883495145631066 gives 643,649.7392030944 in today's dollars; multiplying by 1.03^30 gives the 1,562,306.8565586845 nominal figure. The nominal recurrence B_k = B_{k-1}(1.07) + 6000(1.03)^k reproduces both to floating-point noise, which is what makes this an identity rather than an approximation.

cases.description: The same plan with flat nominal contributions.
cases.derivation: B_k = B_{k-1}(1.07) + 6000 with no escalation, deflated by 1.03^30 at the end. Total invested is exactly 100,000 + 30*6,000 = 280,000 because nothing escalates.

cases.description: Retiring at 55 with Medicare at 65 leaves a 10 year self-funded gap.
cases.derivation: annualCost = 600*12 + 2,500 + 2,000 = 11,700. Costs inflate from year zero, so the total is the geometric sum A*((1+i)^n - 1)/i = 11,700*(1.03^10 - 1)/0.03 = 134,126.6, which rounds to 134,127.

cases.description: Retiring at or after Medicare eligibility leaves no gap at all.
cases.derivation: gapYears = max(0, 65 - 67) = 0, so the total is an empty sum and the average is defined as zero rather than a division by zero.

cases.description: A fifty-cent annual shortfall: the exact input that made web and MAUI give opposite verdicts before issue #63.
cases.derivation: Flat plan, chosen so every intermediate value is exact and the surplus can be derived by hand. inflationRate is 0, so inflationMultiplier = (1+0)^k = 1 for every year and expenses = annualExpenses exactly. There are no accounts, so deferredIncome and portfolioWithdrawals are both 0 and totalIncome is the pension alone. The pension is after-tax with annualGrowth 0 and is active across the whole span, so its nominal amount is 10000*(1+0)^k = 10000 exactly every year. Therefore surplus = 10000 - annualExpenses, identically in each of the three projected years. annualExpenses = 10000.50, so surplus = 10000 - 10000.50 = -0.50 exactly; 10000 and 10000.5 are both exactly representable in binary64 (10000.5 = 20001/2), so this is a true midpoint and not floating-point noise. Rounded away from zero for display, -0.50 becomes -1. The verdict is taken from the unrounded value against a half-dollar tolerance: -0.50 <= -0.50 is true, so all three years are short, giving fundedYears 0, firstShortfallAge 60 and yearsFullyCovered 0. expenses displays as round(10000.50) = 10001 (the positive midpoint rounds the same way under both platforms' rules). Before the fix web produced Math.round(-0.5) = -0, and -0 < 0 is false, so it reported fundedYears 3 and firstShortfallAge null.

cases.description: A $2.50 annual shortfall, the midpoint where the two platforms' rounding rules differed by a whole dollar.
cases.derivation: Flat plan, chosen so every intermediate value is exact and the surplus can be derived by hand. inflationRate is 0, so inflationMultiplier = (1+0)^k = 1 for every year and expenses = annualExpenses exactly. There are no accounts, so deferredIncome and portfolioWithdrawals are both 0 and totalIncome is the pension alone. The pension is after-tax with annualGrowth 0 and is active across the whole span, so its nominal amount is 10000*(1+0)^k = 10000 exactly every year. Therefore surplus = 10000 - annualExpenses, identically in each of the three projected years. annualExpenses = 10002.50, so surplus = 10000 - 10002.50 = -2.50 exactly; both operands are exactly representable in binary64 (10002.5 = 20005/2). Rounded away from zero, -2.50 becomes -3; the bare JS Math.round web used before issue #63 rounds half toward +Infinity and produced -2. The verdict is unaffected by which of the two a platform picked, since -2.50 <= -0.50 either way: all three years are short, so fundedYears 0, firstShortfallAge 60, yearsFullyCovered 0. expenses displays as round(10002.50) = 10003.

cases.description: A $2.50 annual surplus: the positive midpoint, where the two rounding rules always agreed.
cases.derivation: Flat plan, chosen so every intermediate value is exact and the surplus can be derived by hand. inflationRate is 0, so inflationMultiplier = (1+0)^k = 1 for every year and expenses = annualExpenses exactly. There are no accounts, so deferredIncome and portfolioWithdrawals are both 0 and totalIncome is the pension alone. The pension is after-tax with annualGrowth 0 and is active across the whole span, so its nominal amount is 10000*(1+0)^k = 10000 exactly every year. Therefore surplus = 10000 - annualExpenses, identically in each of the three projected years. annualExpenses = 9997.50, so surplus = 10000 - 9997.50 = +2.50 exactly (9997.5 = 19995/2, exactly representable). Math.round(2.5) is 3 and MidpointRounding.AwayFromZero also gives 3 — the two rules differ only on negatives, which is why issue #63 went unnoticed for so long. +2.50 > -0.50, so no year is short: fundedYears 3, firstShortfallAge null, yearsFullyCovered 3. expenses displays as round(9997.50) = 9998.

cases.description: A forty-cent annual gap: inside the half-dollar tolerance, so it displays as $0 and reads as funded on both platforms.
cases.derivation: Flat plan, chosen so every intermediate value is exact and the surplus can be derived by hand. inflationRate is 0, so inflationMultiplier = (1+0)^k = 1 for every year and expenses = annualExpenses exactly. There are no accounts, so deferredIncome and portfolioWithdrawals are both 0 and totalIncome is the pension alone. The pension is after-tax with annualGrowth 0 and is active across the whole span, so its nominal amount is 10000*(1+0)^k = 10000 exactly every year. Therefore surplus = 10000 - annualExpenses, identically in each of the three projected years. annualExpenses = 10000.40, so surplus = 10000 - 10000.40 = -0.40. Unlike the other three cases this is NOT an exact midpoint: 10000.4 has no exact binary64 representation, so the stored surplus is about -0.4000000000000909. That representation error is around 9e-14 and the conclusion is insensitive to it, because the value is a tenth of a dollar clear of the -0.50 tolerance on one side and of the -0.50 rounding boundary on the other. Rounded away from zero, -0.40 becomes NEGATIVE zero, which C# ToString("C0") renders as "-$0" and Intl.NumberFormat renders as "-$0"; both platforms now normalise it to positive zero, so surplus is 0 and not -0. -0.40 > -0.50, so no year is short: fundedYears 3, firstShortfallAge null, yearsFullyCovered 3. This case pins the documented cost of a whole-dollar calculator — a sub-fifty-cent gap is reported as funded — and pins it as agreement rather than per-platform behaviour. expenses displays as round(10000.40) = 10000.

cases.description: A 4% withdrawal rate that cannot fund the year: the cap flexes so the plan spends what it needs instead of reporting a shortfall beside an untouched balance.
cases.derivation: Chosen so every value is exact in binary64 and the whole three-year path can be walked by hand. inflationRate is 0, so expenses = annualExpenses = 10000 every year; annualReturn is 0 and annualContribution is 0, so a balance only ever changes by what is withdrawn. There is no income and no deferred account, so the entire 10000 gap must come from the one taxable account, whose withdrawalTaxRate is 0 — gross equals net, and the tax gross-up is deliberately kept out of this case (deferred-cap-flex-prorates-and-skips-locked-accounts covers it). Age 60 is the start age, so no growth is applied and the balance is the entered 100000. POLICY PASS: policyLimit = 100000*0.04 = 4000, which is below the 10000 needed, so it takes 4000 and leaves remainingGap = 6000. That 6000 is at or beyond the half-dollar tolerance, so the year would have been reported short and the flex pass runs. FLEX PASS: the reachable balance is now 96000 and netCapacity = 96000*1 = 96000; flexScale = min(6000, 96000)/96000 = 0.0625, so gross = 96000*0.0625 = 6000 exactly. Total withdrawn is 4000+6000 = 10000, the balance falls to exactly 90000, and surplus = 10000-10000 = 0, so the year is FUNDED and policyExcessWithdrawals is the 6000 taken above policy. The same walk repeats on a balance that is 10000 lower each year: age 61 takes 3600 by policy and flexes 6400 (netCapacity 86400, scale 6400/86400) to reach 80000; age 62 takes 3200 and flexes 6800 (netCapacity 76800) to reach 70000. Because every year is fully covered, fundedYears is 3, firstShortfallAge is null and yearsFullyCovered is 3; balanceAtSemiRetirement is the age-60 total of 90000 and endingBalance is the age-62 total of 70000. THIS IS THE CASE THAT WOULD HAVE FAILED BEFORE ISSUE #56: the old engine withdrew only the capped 4000/3840/3686, reported surplus -6000/-6160/-6314 and fundedYears 0, and left 88474 sitting in the account it had just declared the user could not live on.

cases.description: Flexed withdrawals prorate across reachable accounts in proportion to balance, gross up for each account's withdrawal tax, and never touch an account below its availableAge.
cases.derivation: NOTE THE WITHDRAWAL RATES: every account is entered with withdrawalRate 0, so the policy pass takes nothing at all and the numbers below isolate the flex pass exactly. A reader who assumes the 4% default will derive different figures and wrongly conclude the fixture is broken. One projected year (currentAge = semiRetirementAge = planThroughAge = 60) with inflationRate 0, annualReturn 0 and annualContribution 0, so no growth is applied and the entered balances are the balances. Expenses are 10000; there is no income, so the whole 10000 is the gap. REACHABILITY: 'taxfree' and 'taxed' have availableAge 60 and are reachable; 'locked' has availableAge 70 and is not, so it must end the year holding its full 100000 — the locked-account rule is a real constraint and the flex does not get to break it. FLEX PASS: netCapacity is the SPENDABLE capacity of the reachable accounts, 50000*(1-0) + 40000*(1-0.25) = 50000 + 30000 = 80000. flexScale = min(10000, 80000)/80000 = 0.125, exactly representable as one eighth. Gross withdrawals are balance*flexScale: taxfree 50000*0.125 = 6250 and taxed 40000*0.125 = 5000. BOTH ARE 12.5% OF THEIR OWN BALANCE, which is the proration rule being pinned — gross is proportional to balance, mirroring distributeSurplus, which prorates a surplus back in by balance. Spendable: 6250*1 = 6250 plus 5000*0.75 = 3750, totalling exactly 10000, so surplus = 0 and the year is funded; withdrawalTaxes = 5000*0.25 = 1250. Ending balances are 43750, 35000 and the untouched 100000, so totalBalance = 178750, which is also balanceAtSemiRetirement and endingBalance because there is only one year. THE ENDING BALANCE IS WHAT PINS THE ORDERING POLICY: a taxable-first rule would have taken the whole 10000 gross from the tax-free account and left 40000 + 40000 + 100000 = 180000. A proration rule that no expected value distinguishes from its alternative is not actually pinned, so 178750 rather than 180000 is the assertion that defends this choice. policyExcessWithdrawals is the total gross taken above policy, 6250 + 5000 = 11250 (policy allowed 0).

cases.description: Flexing is bounded by the money that exists: the account empties to exactly zero and the year is still reported short.
cases.derivation: One projected year (currentAge = semiRetirementAge = planThroughAge = 60), inflationRate 0, annualReturn 0, annualContribution 0, so the balance is the entered 30000 and expenses are the entered 100000. There is no income, so the gap is the full 100000 against one reachable untaxed account holding 30000. POLICY PASS: policyLimit = 30000*0.04 = 1200, below the amount needed, so it takes 1200 and leaves remainingGap = 98800, well past the half-dollar tolerance, so the flex pass runs. FLEX PASS: the remaining balance is 28800 and netCapacity = 28800*1 = 28800. The scale is taken from min(remainingGap, netCapacity) = min(98800, 28800) = 28800, so flexScale = 28800/28800 = 1 EXACTLY — the bound at 1 is the structural reason a balance can never go negative, and here it binds. Gross = 28800*1 = 28800 and the balance lands on exactly 0 rather than a floating-point residue. Total withdrawn is 1200 + 28800 = 30000, which is the whole account, so totalIncome = 30000 against 100000 of expenses and surplus = -70000. -70000 <= -0.5, so the year IS short: fundedYears 0, firstShortfallAge 60, yearsFullyCovered 0, endingBalance 0. This is the shape the default scenario now ends in, and it is the honest one — the plan falls short because the reachable money is gone, not because a self-imposed rate throttled it. policyExcessWithdrawals is the 28800 taken above the 1200 policy allowed.

cases.description: The withdrawal rate still governs a year the plan can afford: no shortfall means no flex, and nothing is taken above policy.
cases.derivation: The negative control for the three cases above, and the reason the flex is gated rather than unconditional. One projected year (currentAge = semiRetirementAge = planThroughAge = 60), inflationRate 0, annualReturn 0, annualContribution 0, so the balance is the entered 100000 and expenses are the entered 1000. There is no income, so the gap is 1000. POLICY PASS: the account is untaxed, so netFactor is 1 and grossNeeded = 1000/1 = 1000; policyLimit = 100000*0.04 = 4000. The withdrawal is min(balance, grossNeeded, policyLimit) = min(100000, 1000, 4000) = 1000, i.e. the NEED binds, not the cap. remainingGap is then 0. FLEX GATE: the gate asks the same isShortfall question the headline verdict asks, of the unflexed gap: -0 <= -0.5 is false, so the flex pass never runs, policyExcessWithdrawals is 0 and the stated 4% policy is left fully in force. This is what stops the fix from silently converting the withdrawal rate into a no-op field: it is still a real constraint in every year the plan can afford, and it is only exceeded where the alternative is reporting a shortfall beside money the user has. Balance falls to 99000, surplus = 1000-1000 = 0, so the year is funded: fundedYears 1, firstShortfallAge null, endingBalance 99000.
